title: Plane figures and polygon vocabulary
lead: Before measuring a shape, be precise about its boundary. Learn which figures count as polygons and how to name their parts.
outcomes: Identify the sides, vertices, and diagonals of a simple polygon.
Distinguish a convex polygon from a concave polygon.
Explain why a regular polygon must be both equilateral and equiangular.

concepts.heading: A polygon is a closed chain of straight segments.
paragraphs: A plane figure lies in a flat, two-dimensional plane. A simple polygon is a closed figure made from at least three straight line segments. Adjacent sides meet at vertices; nonadjacent sides do not cross.
An open chain is not closed. A curved boundary is not made only of straight segments. A self-crossing chain is not a simple polygon.

concepts.heading: Convexity describes where the vertices point.
paragraphs: A convex polygon has every interior angle less than $180^\circ$. A concave polygon has at least one interior angle greater than $180^\circ$. Both can be simple polygons.
A diagonal joins two nonadjacent vertices. In a triangle every pair of vertices is adjacent, so it has no diagonals.

concepts.heading: Regular means equal sides and equal angles.
paragraphs: An equilateral polygon has all sides equal; an equiangular polygon has all interior angles equal. A regular polygon has both properties.
A rhombus need not be regular because its angles can differ. A rectangle need not be regular because its side lengths can differ. A square is both.

vocabulary.definition: A straight segment forming part of a polygon's boundary.
A point where two adjacent sides meet.
A segment joining two nonadjacent vertices.
A simple polygon whose interior angles are all less than $180^\circ$.
A simple polygon with at least one interior angle greater than $180^\circ$.
For a regular polygon, the perpendicular segment from its center to a side; it meets the side at its midpoint.
